title: Talking about God (ST I.13)
hookLine: God is good, but not in exactly the way we are good

cards: A girl back from her first trip to the coast is on the phone with an inland friend who's never seen the sea. It's like the lake, she says. But bigger.
No, way bigger, you can't see the other side. And it moves by itself. And it's salty, and loud.

She keeps reaching for words her friend already has, and every one is true, and every one falls short. Thomas Aquinas has the same problem, only harder. Every word we have, we learned from things around us.
So what can good, or wise, mean of God? Today's word is his answer.

teach.b: Thomas sees two dead ends. The first: our words mean exactly the same of God as of us. God is good like a kind neighbor, just more so.
But then God is one more thing among things, only larger, and yesterday Thomas said God isn't built like anything we know.
The second: our words mean something totally different of God, the way a river bank and a savings bank share only a spelling.
But then, Thomas says, we could know nothing about God, and every argument we've walked would be empty. So he takes a middle road, and calls it analogy. His example is healthy.
A person is healthy. A meal is healthy, because it brings health. A face looks healthy, because it shows health.
Same word, not the same meaning, and not unrelated either; each use points to the one health. God is good. Thomas insists this doesn't merely mean God causes good things, or isn't bad.
Goodness is really in God, in a higher way. Then he flips the picture.
We learn good from good things around us, so the word feels like ours first.
But as to what it means, Thomas says, it belongs to God first, and to us by sharing.

teach.h: OF WHOM ALL PATERNITY IS NAMED.
teach.b: He points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, praying to the Father "of whom all paternity in heaven and earth is named." We learned father from our fathers. Paul says fatherhood is named from God.
So for Thomas, our words aren't wrong about God. They're true, and too small. God is like what they say, and more.

how: Catholic theology uses Thomas's teaching on analogy to explain how words like good, wise and father can be said truly of God while God remains beyond them; readers meet it in the Summa's question on the names of God.

o: words said of God and us in just the same sense
a story that compares God to a human king
words said of God in a related sense, true but small

games.q: talking about God — tap the pairs.

s: Thomas says 'God is good' only means God causes good things
he says goodness is really in God, in a higher way.
Thomas says words like good and wise mean exactly the same of God as of us
not the same sense, and not a totally different one: an analogy.
Thomas says that, as to what they mean, such words belong to God first
we learn them from creatures first, but the reality is God's first; Paul says all fatherhood is named from God.

games.q: someone says, God is good. what does Thomas think those words can mean?
o: good in exactly the way a kind neighbor is good, only bigger.
good in a sense with no link to our goodness at all.
truly good, like our goodness, and beyond it.
games.why: Thomas rejects both the same sense and a totally different sense. the word is used by analogy: true of God, in a higher way, and God's first.

practice: Pick one word you'd use of God, or of whatever is largest in your life, good, faithful, father, light, and remember where you first learned it: a person, a morning, a kitchen.
Let it be true, then let it stretch, noticing where your memory of it falls short, and stay between like and unlike. If you pray, speak the word quietly to God, and let it be too small.

wordCard.voice: Analogy. Thomas Aquinas's way of speaking of God: our words are not used in exactly the same sense, nor a totally different one, but a related one.

orig.note: Latin, from Greek: proportion — Thomas says names are said of God and creatures by analogy, that is, by proportion.

carryVoice: Your line: like, and more. Our words for God all point past themselves. Until tomorrow.
